title: The Elevator
author: William Sleator
tagline: A frightened boy, a cramped lift, and a silent woman whose 'Hello, Martin' turns an ordinary building into a trap.

overview.intro: Twelve-year-old Martin has moved with his father to an apartment on the seventeenth floor of an old building, and he is afraid of its tiny, shuddering elevator. His fear is dismissed by everyone he tries to tell — until a large, silent woman begins appearing in the lift at impossible moments and seems to know exactly who he is. Sleator builds suspense out of the most ordinary space imaginable: a metal box that stops at floors it was never asked to choose.

learn.title: Before you read: why elevators frighten us

blocks.text: Suspense writing often uses confined, everyday spaces — corridors, lifts, stairwells — because their familiarity makes the intrusion of fear more shocking. An elevator concentrates everything an anxious person dislikes: darkness, smallness, no exit, no control over movement, and company you did not choose. Sleator exploits each of these properties in turn, and he adds the one ingredient that turns discomfort into dread: the woman in the lift behaves as if she has been watching Martin for a long time.

As you read, track two threads side by side. The first is physical: which floor the elevator stops at, who enters, where Martin's father is at each moment. The second is emotional: how Martin's fear grows each time the adults around him refuse to take it seriously. The story's real engine is the gap between what Martin knows and what the adults will acknowledge.

Martin, twelve, thin and fearful, has moved with his father to an old building, flat 17A. From the first page he distrusts the elevator: it is cramped, it shudders, and the dark stairwell seems no better. His father tells him to grow up and use the lift like everyone else. On one ride, a large silent woman boards at the fourteenth floor and stares at Martin without speaking. Later she boards at the third floor and presses the button for the eighteenth — not her floor, and past Martin's — so that when he gets out he believes she now knows where he lives.

items: Martin tells his father about the woman; his father scolds him and thinks nothing of it.
The next morning the woman is already standing in the elevator before Martin opens the door.
Martin panics and runs for the stairs, falls, and breaks his leg — the fear has produced the exact helplessness it promised.
After the hospital, his father leaves Martin alone on crutches in the elevator to visit a neighbour on the ninth floor.
At the tenth floor the woman enters, stops the elevator, and says, 'Hello, Martin' — and the story ends there.
The final line confirms that she knows his name, his floor, and his routines: everything Martin feared is suddenly verified.

items.text: The woman presses for the eighteenth floor while riding from the third.
items.note: A deliberate over-shoot of Martin's floor: the story's first evidence that her movements are calculated rather than accidental.

items.text: Martin's father leaves him alone in the lift to visit Mrs. Ullman on the ninth floor.
items.note: The adults' carelessness removes Martin's protection at the moment the pattern has already been established.

blocks.text: Martin embodies ordinary, believable childhood anxiety. He is perceptive — he notices the woman's floors, her staring, her timing — but he lacks the standing to make anyone listen. Sleator never mocks him: the story validates every detail Martin observes, so his fear reads as accuracy rather than fantasy. His broken leg is the cruellest turn of the plot, because it removes the one defence he had left, the stairs.

Martin's father represents the adult refusal to hear what children say. He does not disbelieve Martin so much as decline to consider him; 'grow up' is his answer to evidence. His exit from the elevator on the ninth floor is not malice but inattention — which is precisely the story's point: inattentive adults hand the child over to the thing he fears. The large woman remains unexplained throughout: she never hurries, never justifies herself, and her single spoken line — his name — does more damage than any action.

items.meaning: Twelve-year-old protagonist: slight, anxious, observant, and disbelieved.
A silent, unsettling stranger whose knowledge of Martin's name drives the suspense.
Unsympathetic and impatient with fear; his dismissals leave Martin unprotected.
The neighbour whose flat takes Martin's father out of the elevator on the ninth floor.
Martin's only real defence after the fall — and what makes the final ride inescapable.

blocks.text: The story works by a pattern of repetition with escalation. Each encounter with the woman is worse than the last: a stare at the fourteenth, an over-shot button to the eighteenth, presence in the lift before dawn, and finally speech. Between these escalations Sleator inserts false safety — the father's mockery, the ordinary morning, the neighbour's flat — so that the reader relaxes at exactly the moments Martin should not. The elevator itself is a suspense device: it moves when someone else decides, stops where someone else chooses, and seals the doors on choices already made.

blocks.caption: The escalation of encounters
rows: Boards at the fourteenth and stares in silence
Unsettlement: staring is impolite but explainable — barely
Boards at the third and presses the eighteenth
Fear with evidence: she has learned his floor
Is already inside before Martin opens the door

items: Setting does half the work: a shuddering box, a dark stairwell, floors without names.
Dramatic irony: the reader counts the floors with Martin while the adults count nothing.
The father's dismissal functions as a countdown — each ignored warning leaves Martin more exposed.
Silence is the woman's instrument; her single line of dialogue lands with enormous weight.
The broken leg converts fear into fact: Martin loses the stairs at the exact moment he needs them.

blocks.text: Fear and its dismissal form the story's central pair. Martin's anxiety is treated by his father as an immaturity to be outgrown, and the narrative quietly proves the boy right at every step. The story therefore argues that children's fears deserve examination rather than ridicule: every detail Martin reports turns out to be true, and it is the adults' refusal to check that leaves him trapped. Fear, in other words, is not the horror here — being unheard is.

Isolation runs through the plot like a second theme. Martin has no friend, no mother, no sibling and no teacher in the story; the only person who might listen is his father, who does not. The elevator magnifies this: a locked box with a stranger in it is the physical form of having no one to turn to. Even the building's architecture keeps people adjacent but unconnected — neighbours on other floors, doors that close between them — until the woman, the one person who finally 'connects' with Martin, does so as a threat.

items: Fear versus dismissal: the child perceives correctly and is punished for saying so.
Isolation: Martin faces everything alone, with no believing adult in reach.
Vulnerability: smallness, injury and confinement make defence impossible.
The unknown: the woman is never explained, because explanation would release the tension the story is built on.
Growth demanded too early: 'grow up' is the father's answer, and the story shows its cost.

learn.title: Reading and writing tips for this story

blocks.text: Suspense questions reward precision: track floors, timings and entrances, because the examiner's favourite evidence is the woman's pattern of stops. When writing about the ending, remember that the story deliberately withholds an explanation — your job is to argue from what the text gives you (her knowledge of his name, her timing, his aloneness) rather than to invent a backstory. For character answers, pair Martin's perception with the adults' inattention; for style answers, concentrate on escalation and the silence of the woman.

items: Make a four-row table of encounters before answering any suspense question.
When asked about setting, name the three confined spaces: elevator, stairwell, hallway.
The father's lines are short and dismissive — quote the pattern of them, not one line in isolation.
For the open ending, offer an interpretation and one piece of textual evidence for it; do not pretend the text settles it.

keyPoints: Sleator never explains the woman: her power comes from silence, timing and the single word 'Martin'.
Suspense is built by escalation — each encounter adds knowledge and removes one of Martin's options.
The elevator is a suspense machine: it stops for others, moves for others, and seals the doors on choices.
Martin's fear is repeatedly validated by the plot; it is the adults, not the boy, who are wrong.
The father's dismissals are the story's countdown: each 'grow up' leaves Martin more exposed.
The broken leg is the pivot of the plot — losing the stairs makes the final ride unavoidable.
Setting is confined on purpose: shaft, stairwell and hallway give nowhere safe to stand.
The ending is open by design; the text confirms danger (she knows his name) but not identity or motive.
Theme: children's fears deserve to be heard — the horror arises from being disbelieved, not from the woman herself.
examFocus: Suspense question: answer with the four-encounter pattern; the examiner wants evidence of escalation, not a plot retell.
Setting question: confined spaces (elevator, stairwell) plus the mechanical helplessness of floors chosen by someone else.
Character: Martin = perceptive and truthful; father = impatient and inattentive; woman = an unexplained force, deliberately unexplained.
Style: name the techniques — escalation, dramatic irony, repetition, withheld information — and illustrate each.
The ending: argue from evidence ('knows the name', 'stops the elevator') and acknowledge what remains unresolved.
Theme answers should connect the woman's appearances to the adults' silence: being unheard is what traps Martin.

questions.prompt: Why is Martin afraid of the building's elevator before he ever meets the woman?
options: It is cramped, shuddering, and he distrusts it — and the dark stairwell seems no better
It once trapped him overnight with no light
His father has forbidden him to use it
It opens only on even-numbered floors
questions.answer: It is cramped, shuddering, and he distrusts it — and the dark stairwell seems no better
questions.explanation: Sleator establishes Martin's fear before the woman appears: the car is small and unsteady, and the alternative, a dark stairwell, offers no comfort either. The fear begins as a sensible response to a bad building, which makes the later escalation believable.
questions.commonMistake: Blaming the woman for Martin's original fear — the text establishes the fear of the lift itself first.

questions.prompt: What happens the morning after Martin's father refuses to take his concerns seriously?
options: The elevator is broken, and Martin takes the stairs in relief
The large woman is already standing inside the elevator when Martin opens the door
His father agrees to move to a lower floor
The woman is waiting outside the building's front door
questions.answer: The large woman is already standing inside the elevator when Martin opens the door
questions.explanation: The escalation reaches surveillance: she is no longer boarding at chosen floors but waiting before Martin has even started his journey. This is the encounter that makes him run for the stairs — and fall.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing this with the second ride (third floor to eighteenth); the morning encounter comes after the father's dismissal.

questions.prompt: Describe the woman's first two appearances in the elevator.
questions.answer: First, she boards at the fourteenth floor and stands staring at Martin without speaking. Next, she boards at the third floor and presses the button for the eighteenth floor — a floor above Martin's, which he has just passed. On both occasions she is silent, large and unreadable, and by the second appearance she appears to have learned where he lives.
questions.explanation: The two appearances must be kept distinct: the stare (unsettling but explainable) and the over-shot button (evidence of intention). Silence characterises both.
questions.commonMistake: Merging the encounters into one — the pattern of repetition with escalation is what the question is testing.

questions.prompt: How does Martin's father react to Martin's fears, and with what consequence?
questions.answer: His father scolds him, tells him to grow up, and dismisses every report of the woman without checking it. The consequence is that Martin is left entirely unprotected: on the morning he runs from the elevator in panic, he falls and breaks his leg, and later his father even leaves him alone in the lift to visit a neighbour. The dismissal does not remove the danger; it removes Martin's defence against it.
questions.explanation: The question links reaction to consequence: dismissal → isolation → injury → abandonment in the elevator. Answers should show the causal chain rather than merely describing the father's attitude.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the father as cruel — he is inattentive, not malicious, and the story's criticism is of carelessness.

questions.prompt: Explain how Sleator uses the elevator itself to create suspense. Refer to at least three details.
questions.answer: The elevator is built as a suspense device. Its movement belongs to other people: it stops where the woman chooses (the fourteenth, the third, the eighteenth) rather than where Martin wants, so every ride is a test of what the next door will reveal. Its space is a metal box too small to retreat within — once the doors close, Martin is sealed with whoever else is inside. Its reliability is doubtful from the first page (it shudders), which makes each hesitation of the car feel like an event. And its routine is finally broken against him: the woman stops it at the tenth floor to speak, choosing the place of the confrontation as carefully as everything else.
questions.explanation: Three details are the minimum: stops chosen by others, the sealed enclosure, and the shuddering unreliability — with the deliberate stop at the tenth as the climax of the pattern.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the woman's actions instead of the mechanics of the lift — the question asks how the space itself generates suspense.

questions.prompt: How does the story show that Martin perceives the danger accurately, even though no adult believes him?
questions.answer: Every detail Martin reports turns out to be true within the plot: the woman does over-shoot his floor, she does appear before he opens the door, and she does know his name. The narration stays close to Martin's perceptions, so the reader verifies each of his observations directly while his father never checks any of them. Even his panic is proportionate — he runs, and the accident that follows proves how real his terror was. Sleator therefore inverts the usual pattern of children's horror stories: the child is the reliable witness, and the adults' failure to listen is what allows the danger to close in.
questions.explanation: The answer must pile up the verified details and contrast them with the father's zero verification. The narrative viewpoint (close third person on Martin) is the structural reason the reader sides with him.
questions.commonMistake: Arguing that Martin 'imagines' the woman — nothing in the text supports that reading; she is physically present each time.

questions.prompt: Discuss how the theme of isolation is developed through the story's people and places.
questions.answer: Isolation is built into the cast: Martin has no friend, no mother and no sibling in the story, and the one adult who might listen refuses to. The places repeat the condition — a flat high in an old building, a dark stairwell, a lift that seals its doors — so that even among neighbours Martin is structurally alone. The father's ninth-floor visit removes the last companion at the moment of greatest risk, leaving Martin on crutches in a box with the woman. Even the woman's method is isolating: she never speaks in public, never appears when the father is present, and addresses Martin only when he is definitively alone.
questions.explanation: A strong theme answer works at two levels: people (absent allies, dismissive father) and places (high flat, sealed elevator, dark stairwell), then shows how the plot exploits both — the ninth-floor exit is where the two levels meet.
questions.commonMistake: Listing lonely details without showing development — the theme must be traced across the plot, not just named.

questions.prompt: What role does Mrs. Ullman play in the story?
questions.answer: Mrs. Ullman is a neighbour mentioned only to explain why Martin's father leaves the elevator on the ninth floor. She has no active part in the central encounters, but her existence sets up the story's final predicament: the father's brief errand is what leaves Martin alone in the lift with the woman at the tenth floor.
questions.explanation: Mrs. Ullman is a structural device rather than a character: identify her as the reason for the father's exit and connect that exit to the final scene.
questions.commonMistake: Inventing a larger role for her — the text gives her only the function of drawing the father away.

questions.prompt: The story ends with the woman saying 'Hello, Martin.' What do you think she wants? Give two possible interpretations and decide which the text better supports.
questions.answer: Interpretation one: she is a figure of simple menace — a predator who has been tracking the boy, learning his floor and his routines, and who finally has him alone and immobile; the use of his name is the triumphant reveal of that pursuit. Interpretation two: she is a neighbour or acquaintance whose odd, silent behaviour has been misread, and who greets him by name simply because she knows the building's residents — in which case Martin's fear, not her intent, is the true danger. The text better supports the first: her stops are calculated (the eighteenth-floor over-shoot), her timing is impossible (already inside before dawn), she chooses moments when he is alone, and the elevator is stopped before she speaks. Yet the story gives her no name, no motive and no history, which keeps interpretation two formally alive and leaves the reader, like Martin, condemned to suspect.
questions.explanation: A discuss answer must offer two readings, test both against evidence (calculated stops, impossible timing, the stopped elevator, the withheld identity), and then commit. Full marks come from the judgement plus the textual anchors, not from certainty the text refuses to give.
questions.commonMistake: Asserting one interpretation as fact — the ending is deliberately open, and the marking rewards weighing evidence.

questions.prompt: 'The real horror of the story is Martin's father.' Write a response arguing for or against this statement.
questions.answer: For: the father is the only person who could have ended the danger at any point — by checking the woman's behaviour, by moving Martin's routine, by simply riding with him. Instead he answers evidence with 'grow up', converts his son's accurate reports into a fault of character, and finally leaves Martin alone in the very lift he fears; without that dismissal the pattern would have been interrupted and the last ride would never have occurred. The story's structure supports the claim: every escalation happens after an ignored warning. Against: the father's carelessness is ordinary, while the woman's behaviour — waiting before dawn, stopping the lift, knowing the name — is extraordinary and deliberate; blaming the adult risks excusing the intentional threat. The stronger reading holds both: the father supplies the opportunity, the woman exploits it, and Sleator's point is that ordinary inattention is what deliberate predators (or deliberate fears) require — the horror is a collaboration between an unlistened-to child and a listening stranger.
questions.explanation: This is an argument question with a built-in counter-position. Credit comes from using plot sequence (escalation follows dismissal) and from the balanced verdict; the best answers keep the father responsible for opportunity without transferring the woman's intent onto him.
questions.commonMistake: Arguing one side only and ignoring the counter — the statement invites debate, and the conclusion should weigh both.
